The future of space colonization - terraforming or space habitats?

I always kinda figured one would naturally lead to the other with enough time and technological innovation. First we figure out how to build orbital habitats, then we move on to seed ships to carry the species from one planet to the next, then once we're on a planet we begin modifying it to suit us.

I think there are a couple of prospects that are commonly overlooked in discussions and articles on this topic. I feel that both terraforming and large rotating habitats are unlikely because they are untenable in scale and time given the shrinking collective attention spans of our society and because they are in competition with two technologies offering vastly cheaper and more immediate prospects; clinical adaptation and artificial intelligence. If we had all the needed technology and means and could start today, building the first rotating colony in space is, at a minimum, a fifty year proposition. Terraforming is a many centuries long proposition. But within even that fifty year span of time we are highly likely to realize either or both clinical solutions to the health issues of 'space wasting' in a microgravity environment and general artificial intelligence. Those two things change the whole ballgame.

With a clinical solution human beings can adapt themselves to the microgravity or lowered gravity environment, precluding the need for vast rotating space habitats that have to be fully constructed before they can be inhabited. That's not normally how we develop places to live --build towns and cities. People are drawn to locations where their independent interests converge, usually because of some logistical attractor in the landscape like access to cheap resources, access to a market, or suitability for nodes of intermodal transfer. (where lower 'bandwidth' short range forms of transportation shift to higher bandwidth longer range forms; road to rail, ship, air) And so, historically, there are no examples of sustainable settlements or cities that were built all-at-once. The usual approach is incremental, the architecture of towns and cities 'emergent' like a termite or ant colony. Big rotating space habitats can't be realized in an emergent fashion, but a microgravity settlement can be. We have the structural technology for that at-hand now. Likewise settlements on the natural bodies. On the Moon or Mars one could build domed spaces--on the surface or underground--that are kilometers wide and filled with garden habitats. So why then would you worry about terraforming the whole thing when you can readily do it, near-term, in a piecemeal fashion?

But then we have that prospect of artificial intelligence in the very same near-term time frame that presents us with another possibility. If clinical solutions to living in space make for much cheaper and quicker habitation, then AI is cheaper still by eliminating humans altogether. AI can travel space by telecommunications, no rockets necessary. Their 'habitats' are data systems needing only electric power and an industrial infrastructure to maintain them. They can be setup easily most anywhere in the solar system. The hardware needs its own transportation, of course, but can use tolerable yield logistics not possible for human transport, leading to vastly reduced deployment cost.

There is always an assumed 'need' for human beings in space. Why? It's pretty well accepted today that human jobs on Earth are being eliminated and may be almost entirely gone within fifty years. Why would space be immune to that same trend? What makes a factory in orbit, on the Moon, or Mars any different from a factory on Earth? Both government and business are compelled, more-or-less, to bottom-line rationalization. Everything they do must be done in the most cost-efficient way. And that leaves no place for human beings once AI arrives. The astronaut will be in the same boat as the burger flipper. Everything government and business might want to do out there will be more cheaply and quickly done by robots. So we're never going to live in space if profit and cost-efficiency are our premises for going there. It won't be nations, governments, or corporations who colonize space. It will be relatively small groups of people who envision some kind of better lifestyle there and can afford, as a community, to create those human habitats that make no economic sense otherwise. And that will depend on leveraging those technologies of clinical adaptation and automation to make that development accessible to small communities. When was the last time you heard anyone from NASA use the word 'lifestyle'?

But community-steading space might take a while to be practical, especially since no one is actually working on, or even considering, that prospect right now. In the meantime, AI will be out there doing everything, slowly increasing in self-management and independence with their increasing sophistication. They will be doing the exploring. They will be doing the science. They will be doing infrastructure building --an infrastructure mostly suiting their needs, not ours. All the while we'll be sitting around on Earth trying to keep the old decrepit dinosaur Industrial Age economies on life-support and pretending to be Captain Kirk and Luke Skywalker in VR, wondering why the future never seems to happen. Then, perhaps, some transhumanist vanguard--perhaps originating with intentional community colonists already accustomed to clinically adapting themselves for the sake of living in space--will start uploading themselves and leaving their wetware behind so they can go join the AIs out there in their native habitat doing the cutting-edge stuff, establishing a transhuman lifestyle as the norm for living in space. And thus data systems, built into enormous solar arrays or buried deep under the surface of natural bodies, become the likely common form of space habitat. VRcos (virtual reality arcologies) where transhumans and AIs live in virtual environments, tele-operate robots outside them, and travel about the solar system by wireless telecom. Strange as it sounds, this might be the more plausible prospect than terraforming planets or building giant elaborate spinning structures.
